title: Open doors
hook: Christian hospitality: the Lord's table, and our kitchen tables

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ and culture: some Christians step back, some set out to change things, some live in two kingdoms at once. Your line was in the world, not of it. Where did you feel both pulls? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

It's the heat of the day, and Abraham is sitting in the doorway of his tent. He looks up, and three men are standing nearby. Genesis tells what happens next, and most of it is running. He runs to meet them. He bows to the ground. He hurries into the tent and asks Sarah to bake bread. He runs to the herd and picks out a calf. Then, the King James Bible says, "he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat." The story has already told us who came to that meal: the Lord appeared to him there. Today closes a week, and it ends at a door left open.
screen: `HE STOOD BY THEM, AND THEY DID EAT.`

segments.voice: The letter to the Hebrews says: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Some readers hear Abraham's tent behind that line. Notice who the guests are. Not old friends. Strangers. The Greek word Hebrews uses is philoxenia, and the King James turns it into a whole phrase: to entertain strangers. The first letter of Peter adds a condition that's harder than it sounds: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Open the door, and don't keep score of what it costs. Christians carry this to two tables. One is the Lord's table, communion. The name itself says whose table it is. Churches differ on what happens there and who may receive: some invite every baptized believer, others ask that those who receive share that church's full faith. This path ranks none of them. The other table is the kitchen table, with its mismatched chairs and a pot of something on the stove. And the door swings both ways. In Revelation, Christ says: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." So look back at this week. Medicine, healing through human hands. Attention, guarding what we look at. Forgiveness that doesn't mean staying in danger. Going to your brother privately first. Blessing enemies. In the world, not of it. And now an open door. Every one of them is about how a life meets other people.
screen: `I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to host someone simply. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who could use a seat at your table. Someone new in town, someone alone, someone you keep meaning to call. Now strip the invitation down. Not a dinner party. A cup of coffee. Toast. A bowl of soup. Notice what argues back: the mess, the time, the fear of awkward silence. Let those voices talk, and keep the picture of the open door. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Open doors. Christian hospitality, from Abraham's tent to the Lord's table to an ordinary kitchen, offered first of all to strangers.
Your line: an open door. Today, invite one person to something simple, a coffee, a meal, a seat at your table. Don't wait until the house is clean. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Christians practice hospitality at the Lord's table in worship and at home, sharing meals with neighbors, newcomers and people in need; some congregations also run community meals and coffee hours open to anyone.

original.note: Greek, Hebrews 13:2: hospitality. the King James renders it "to entertain strangers."

trapdoor: what you thought: hospitality means a spotless home and a good menu.
what it means: an open door, especially to strangers, offered without grudging, from Abraham's tent to the Lord's table to a plain kitchen.
what a scholar hears: philoxenia in Hebrews 13:2, which the King James turns into a phrase: "to entertain strangers."
